object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer as represented in the billing system; identified by account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A distinct product offered, identified by product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Price Plan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that determines what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: Feature Bundle
object_types.definition: The feature set / entitlement bundle a customer gets (seats, API, SSO, etc.), identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Plan Change
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with an effective date and requester, distinct from the subscription's current state.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: Start Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: End Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front.

object_types.name: Billing Period
object_types.definition: The cycle on which a subscription is billed.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.
Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.
Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: Paused Flag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration, overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: Effective Date
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; a derived value, not stored, computed from price plan price normalised to a month.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.
Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan.
Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three different concepts: the billing artefact (Price Plan / plan code), the feature bundle (what the customer gets), and a sales-negotiated deal mentioned by Tom but never modeled or defined. It's unclear if the sales 'deal' concept needs to be part of this model at all.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that. ... It won't. But it'll at least name them separately, which is a start.

ambiguities.description: Whether an account that closes and later returns (same company, new account number) should be modeled as the same real-world Customer entity or genuinely treated as separate Account entities is left as a deliberate business rule with product team disagreement; no separate 'Company' concept was introduced despite Tom's objection.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history. ... It drives finance the other way.

ambiguities.description: The Paused flag overlaps semantically with Status (a subscription can be 'active' and 'paused' simultaneously) causing acknowledged bugs; it's unclear whether Paused should be modeled as a true independent boolean attribute or as an additional status value, and the transcript explicitly declines to resolve this cleanly.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs. prorated refund vs. credit) is explicitly undecided and parked; only the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured, with manual credits happening outside the system as an unresolved policy gap.

source_references.excerpt: There's a system behaviour: cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues. There's no refund mechanism at all... ... Put my name on wanting that resolved.

ambiguities.description: Sam initially states the subscription's plan is fully derived from plan change history (no current price plan field), then Priya corrects this to say there IS a denormalised current plan field maintained by the change process, and Sam withdraws his correction. This reveals a genuine risk of stale/undocumented schema knowledge among stakeholders, and raises the question of what happens if the denormalised field and the change history ever diverge (acknowledged as a 'bug' scenario, not a hard constraint).

source_references.excerpt: One correction. You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really... ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field... ... Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: MRR is explicitly stated to be a derived/calculated value from price plan price and billing period, not a stored fact, so it is intentionally NOT modeled as a fact type relating Subscription to a stored attribute -- this is a modeling decision flagged during the session rather than a fact to be captured directly.

source_references.excerpt: So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether Feature Bundle can exist without any Price Plan pointing to it as a permanent state (e.g. Enterprise existed for two months unpriced) versus this being a temporary/transitional condition only -- the min cardinality of Price Plan-per-Bundle (0 vs some minimum over time) is not fully pinned down as a hard constraint.

source_references.excerpt: And can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it? ... Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.
